client: Hey Luna, it's been a tough couple of months. Since graduating in May, I've been struggling to find a job in my field, and it's really starting to get to me. I see my peers landing great positions, and I can't help but feel like I'm falling behind or not good enough. I'm not even sure if therapy can really help with this.
therapist: Hi there, it sounds like you're really going through a tough time, and feeling stuck can be incredibly challenging. It's completely understandable to feel this way, especially when you see others moving forward. What are some thoughts that come up for you when you compare yourself to your peers?

client: Yeah, it's tough. When I see my friends or peers doing so well in their careers or relationships, I just feel like I'm falling behind. It makes me wonder if I'm doing something wrong or if I'm just not good enough. It's hard not to take it personally.
therapist: It sounds like those comparisons are really weighing on you, and it’s natural to question yourself when you see others succeeding. It’s important to remember that everyone’s journey is different, and sometimes it can take a bit longer to find the right path. What are some strengths or achievements of yours that you might be overlooking right now?

client: I know, but it's hard not to feel like I'm falling behind when I see everyone else moving forward. I guess I do have a few things I'm proud of, like finishing that online course and getting that small freelance gig, but they feel so small compared to what others are doing. It's just tough to see those as real achievements when I feel like I should be doing so much more.
therapist: It’s completely understandable to feel that way, and it’s great that you’ve acknowledged some of your own accomplishments, even if they feel small right now. Recognizing those achievements is an important step. Can you think of any specific reasons why those accomplishments are valuable to you, or any skills you developed through them?

client: I guess I can see the value in those small accomplishments, but it’s hard to feel proud of them when I’m constantly comparing myself to others. It feels like everyone else is doing so much more, you know? I’m not sure if focusing on these small wins will really make a difference in how I feel.
therapist: I can see how challenging it is to feel proud of your accomplishments when you’re constantly comparing yourself to others. It’s a common struggle, and it’s important to recognize that everyone’s journey is unique. Focusing on your small wins can build your confidence over time, and it might help to set some realistic goals for yourself that feel meaningful. What are some short-term goals you could set that might help you feel more in control of your progress?

client: I understand what you're saying, but it's hard for me to see my progress when I feel like everyone around me is doing so much better. Setting goals sounds good in theory, but I worry that I'll just set them too high and end up feeling disappointed again. It's tough to find that balance.
therapist: I can see how setting goals might feel daunting when you’re already feeling down. It’s totally understandable to worry about setting yourself up for disappointment. One approach could be to start with very small, achievable goals that build on each other. This can help you see tangible progress and gradually boost your confidence. What are some tiny steps you could take that feel manageable and meaningful to you?

client: I understand what you're saying, and I really appreciate the idea of starting small. But it's hard for me to even figure out what those tiny steps could be. I feel like I've tried setting small goals before, and they still didn't feel achievable, which just made me feel worse. How do I know I won’t end up feeling the same way again?
therapist: I understand that setting goals, even small ones, can feel overwhelming, especially when you’ve had experiences that didn’t turn out as you hoped. It’s important to be gentle with yourself and recognize that it’s okay to feel uncertain. One approach could be to start with very simple, daily actions that feel just a little bit outside your comfort zone. For example, you might spend 10 minutes each day updating your resume or reaching out to one professional contact. What do you think about trying something like that, and how does it feel compared to your past goal-setting experiences?

client: I appreciate the idea of starting small, but I still feel a bit overwhelmed. It’s hard because I’ve set goals before and they didn’t work out, which makes me skeptical that this will be any different. I worry that even these small steps might end up feeling too much, and I’ll just end up feeling disappointed again.
therapist: I can really understand how past experiences with goals not working out can make you feel skeptical and overwhelmed. It’s important to acknowledge those feelings and recognize that it’s okay to take things very slowly. Maybe we can focus on just one tiny, manageable step for now, something that feels almost too easy to fail at. How about identifying one small thing you can do today that feels just a little bit better than doing nothing at all? What might that be?

client: I appreciate you understanding how I feel. It’s just hard to even think of something small that won’t make me feel like I’m failing again. I guess I could try to go for a short walk or something, but I’m worried it won’t make a difference and I’ll just end up feeling more frustrated.
therapist: I completely understand how challenging it can be to even consider small steps when you’re feeling this way. It’s natural to worry that they won’t make a difference. Starting with something as simple as a short walk can be a gentle way to take a step forward, and it’s okay if it feels small. What might help you feel a bit more positive about taking that walk, even if it’s just for a few minutes? Could you think of something you enjoy doing afterward, like listening to a favorite song or podcast?

client: I appreciate that, Luna. It’s just hard to get motivated when I feel so overwhelmed. I mean, I know a walk could be good for me, but it feels like such a big hurdle to even put on my shoes. Maybe I could try it, but I’m not sure what would make it feel less daunting. Listening to a podcast sounds nice, but I’m still not sure it will be enough to get me moving.
therapist: I understand that even the smallest steps can feel like big hurdles when you’re feeling overwhelmed. It’s completely okay to take things at your own pace. Maybe we can break it down even further. How about just putting on your shoes for now, and then you can decide if you want to take the walk later? Or, if you do decide to go for a walk, you could start with just a few minutes and see how you feel. What do you think about that?

client: I appreciate you breaking it down, Luna. It does feel more manageable, but I still worry that even just putting on my shoes won't stick. I often find myself starting with good intentions but then getting stuck in my head and not following through. What if I put on my shoes and still end up not going outside?
therapist: I can see how even the smallest steps can feel challenging when you’re dealing with these worries. It’s completely normal to have those fears, and it’s great that you’re being honest about them. Maybe we can focus on the intention itself for now. Putting on your shoes could be a symbolic step toward taking care of yourself, even if you don’t end up going outside. How does it feel to view it that way, as a small victory in itself? And if you do decide to go further, you can always reassess how you feel in the moment. What do you think about that approach?
